name: musl libc
summary: A portable C standard library and POSIX-oriented runtime with an integrated dynamic linker, thread implementation, allocator, and architecture-specific system boundary.

features.name: Portable C and POSIX interface
features.description: musl presents a standard C library implementation with POSIX support, and its source separates common interfaces from architecture-specific code and system-call details.
benefits: Gives applications a stable library-facing boundary across supported architectures
Keeps much of the API and implementation shared across targets
costs: The interface remains constrained by platform and standards compatibility
Architecture-specific behavior must be maintained at the low-level boundary

features.name: Integrated linker and program-startup boundary
features.description: The musl source includes an ldso dynamic linker and startup/environment code alongside libc, while the project documentation explicitly describes static linking as a supported deployment mode.
benefits: Supports both statically linked deployment and dynamic loading within one libc project
Keeps process startup and library loading behavior close to the runtime implementation
costs: Static and dynamic deployment have different dependency and update boundaries
Loader behavior must account for executable, shared object, and TLS layout details

features.name: Thread-local runtime and allocator
features.description: The fixed source contains pthread and thread-local state initialization, errno and stdio access through the current thread, and a malloc implementation with synchronization support for multi-threaded use.
benefits: Provides library services whose state follows process and thread execution
Packages allocation and threading primitives behind the libc boundary
costs: Thread-local state and synchronization add lifecycle and memory-ordering obligations
Allocator behavior remains a runtime performance and fragmentation concern

mathematical_views.question: How are portable C/POSIX operations related to architecture-specific system-call and ABI implementations?
assumptions: Portable interfaces are modeled as abstract operations and architecture code as their target-specific realization
The relation abstracts compiler ABI details and kernel implementation internals
A shared interface does not imply identical timing, errors, or platform capabilities

mathematical_views.question: What runtime state transitions distinguish static startup, dynamic loading, thread creation, and thread-local cleanup?
assumptions: A process is modeled as states containing loaded objects, thread descriptors, and allocator state
Transitions abstract architecture-specific instruction sequences and kernel scheduling
The model compares lifecycle boundaries and does not assert behavioral equivalence between static and dynamic programs

benefits: Portable application-facing C and POSIX boundary
Static and dynamic deployment modes share one project boundary
costs: Linking mode changes dependency, update, and startup assumptions

benefits: Thread and allocation services are available through libc
costs: Synchronization and allocator state complicate runtime reasoning
